decks.title: Application of Integrals — Part 1: Areas under lines and parabolas
goals: Find the area under a curve as a definite integral
Handle curves below or crossing the x-axis
Use horizontal strips for regions beside the y-axis
Find areas bounded by parabolas in standard form and lines parallel to an axis
Use symmetry to shorten the work

slides.heading: Application of Integrals, Part 1
slides.body_md: A definite integral adds up thin strips: that is exactly an area.

visual.alt: The parabola x squared equals 3 y drawn as a U shape through the origin. The region under it, above the x-axis, between x equal to 0 and x equal to 3 is shaded; its top right corner is the point (3, 3).
visual.caption: The shaded region under $x^2 = 3y$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 3$ has area $3$ sq units.

slides.narration: Welcome to application of integrals. A definite integral is more than a number you calculate. It is the sum of many thin strips, and the total of those strips is an area. On the screen, the region under a parabola is shaded. By the end of this part you will find areas like this in a few lines, including regions below the axis and regions beside the y axis.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Write an area as a **definite integral**
Slice with **horizontal strips** when the region sits beside the $y$-axis
Find areas inside **parabolas** cut off by a line parallel to an axis

visual.alt: Table comparing strips. A vertical strip has width d x and length y equal to f of x, and the area is the integral of y d x from a to b. A horizontal strip has width d y and length x equal to g of y, and the area is the integral of x d y from c to d.
visual.caption: Two ways to slice a region into thin strips.

slides.narration: Here are the goals for part one. You will turn a region into an integral, deal with negative values correctly, choose between vertical and horizontal strips, and work with parabolas in standard form. These are the skills behind most two, three and five mark questions in this chapter.

slides.heading: Area as a sum of strips
slides.body_md: Cut the region under $y = f(x) \ge 0$ into vertical strips of width $dx$ and height $y$. Each strip has area $y\,dx$; adding them all from $x = a$ to $x = b$ gives the area.

visual.alt: Table comparing strips. A vertical strip has width d x and length y equal to f of x, and the area is the integral of y d x from a to b. A horizontal strip has width d y and length x equal to g of y, and the area is the integral of x d y from c to d.
visual.caption: Two ways to slice a region into thin strips.

slides.narration: Picture the region under a curve sliced into very thin vertical strips. A strip at position x has height y and a tiny width d x, so its area is y times d x. Add up all the strips from a to b, and the definite integral gives the exact total. Horizontal strips work the same way, with x times d y.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: area under a line
slides.body_md: Find the area bounded by $y = 2x + 1$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x = 1$ and $x = 3$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** The line is above the axis on $[1, 3]$.

visual.alt: The line y equals 2 x plus 1 with the points (1, 3) and (3, 7) marked and vertical lines at x equal to 1 and x equal to 3. The region under the line between them is a trapezium.
visual.caption: Between the ordinates the region is a trapezium: area $10$.

slides.narration: Start with a straight line, where you can check the answer with school geometry. The line two x plus one stays above the axis between one and three, so the area is the integral from one to three. That gives ten square units. The region is a trapezium with parallel sides three and seven and width two, and its area is also ten. The integral agrees with geometry.

slides.heading: The same region, shaded
slides.body_md: The integral measured exactly this trapezium.

visual.alt: The region under the line y equals 2 x plus 1 between x equal to 1 and x equal to 3 shaded: a trapezium with parallel vertical sides of lengths 3 and 7 and width 2.
visual.caption: Trapezium check: $\tfrac12(3 + 7)(2) = 10$.

slides.narration: Here is the region from the example, shaded. Notice the two vertical sides at x equals one and x equals three. They are the limits of the integral. Now try the quick question on the screen: a line through the origin, and a triangle under it. You can check your answer either by integration or by the triangle formula.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: under a parabola
slides.body_md: Find the area of the region bounded by the parabola $x^2 = 3y$, the $x$-axis and the line $x = 3$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Write $y$ in terms of $x$: $y = \dfrac{x^2}{3}$, which is $\ge 0$.

visual.alt: The parabola x squared equals 3 y drawn as a U shape through the origin. The region under it, above the x-axis, between x equal to 0 and x equal to 3 is shaded; its top right corner is the point (3, 3).
visual.caption: The shaded region under $x^2 = 3y$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 3$ has area $3$ sq units.

slides.narration: Now a parabola in standard form, x squared equals three y. First make y the subject: y equals x squared over three. It is never negative, so the region from zero to three lies above the axis. Integrate to get x cubed over nine, and substitute the limits. The area is three square units. Always rewrite the curve as y equals something before you integrate with respect to x.

slides.heading: Quick check: which formula?
slides.body_md: Choose the integral that gives an area under a curve.

visual.alt: Table comparing strips. A vertical strip has width d x and length y equal to f of x, and the area is the integral of y d x from a to b. A horizontal strip has width d y and length x equal to g of y, and the area is the integral of x d y from c to d.
visual.caption: Two ways to slice a region into thin strips.

slides.narration: Take a moment. Which expression gives the area under a curve that stays above the x axis between two vertical lines? Think about what each strip contributes, and do not confuse an area with a change in the function.

slides.heading: When the curve is below the axis
slides.body_md: If $f(x) \le 0$ on $[a, b]$, the integral is **negative**. The area is its absolute value.
bullets: $\displaystyle\int_0^2 (-x^2)\,dx = -\dfrac83$, so the area is $\dfrac83$ sq units

visual.alt: The downward parabola y equals minus x squared. The region between it and the x-axis, from x equal to 0 to x equal to 2, is shaded below the axis, ending at the point (2, minus 4).
visual.caption: $\displaystyle\int_0^2 (-x^2)\,dx = -\dfrac83$, but the shaded area is $\dfrac83$.

slides.narration: When the curve dips below the x axis, each strip has a negative height, so the integral comes out negative. But an area is never negative. Take the absolute value of the integral. For the downward parabola minus x squared from zero to two, the integral is minus eight over three, so the area is eight over three square units.

slides.heading: When the curve crosses the axis
slides.body_md: $y = 2x - 4$ is below the axis on $(0, 2)$ and above it on $(2, 4)$. Split at the crossing point $x = 2$.

visual.alt: The line y equals 2 x minus 4 rising from (0, minus 4) through (2, 0) to (4, 4). It is below the x-axis to the left of 2 and above it to the right.
visual.caption: The line crosses the axis at $x = 2$: split the integral there.

slides.narration: Here is the most common trap in this chapter. The line two x minus four crosses the x axis at two. To the left it is below the axis, and to the right it is above. If you integrate straight from zero to four, the negative part cancels the positive part. So first find where the curve crosses the axis, and split the integral there.

slides.heading: Two triangles, not zero
slides.body_md: Area bounded by $y = 2x - 4$, the $x$-axis, $x = 0$ and $x = 4$.

visual.alt: Two shaded triangles between the line y equals 2 x minus 4 and the x-axis: one below the axis from x equal to 0 to 2, one above the axis from 2 to 4. Each has area 4.
visual.caption: Two triangles of area $4$: total area $8$, although $\displaystyle\int_0^4 (2x - 4)\,dx = 0$.

slides.narration: Work out each part separately. From zero to two the integral is minus four, so that triangle has area four. From two to four the integral is plus four. The total area is eight square units. The single integral from zero to four would give zero, which is the signed, or net, area. Examiners love this question, so always sketch first.

slides.heading: Quick check: a line that crosses
slides.body_md: Find the area; watch for the crossing point.

visual.alt: The line y equals 2 x minus 4 rising from (0, minus 4) through (2, 0) to (4, 4). It is below the x-axis to the left of 2 and above it to the right.
visual.caption: The line crosses the axis at $x = 2$: split the integral there.

slides.narration: Try this one. The line crosses the axis inside the interval. Find the crossing point, work out each part, and add the absolute values. If you get zero, think again.

slides.heading: Parabolas that open sideways
slides.body_md: For $y^2 = kx$ ($k > 0$) the curve is symmetric about the $x$-axis. Upper branch: $y = \sqrt{kx}$; lower branch: $y = -\sqrt{kx}$.
bullets: The region cut off by $x = h$ is twice the region under the upper branch

visual.alt: The two branches of the parabola y squared equals 9 x: y equals 3 root x above the axis and y equals minus 3 root x below it, meeting the line x equal to 4 at (4, 6) and (4, minus 6).
visual.caption: Upper branch $y = 3\sqrt{x}$, lower branch $y = -3\sqrt{x}$.

slides.narration: A parabola like y squared equals nine x opens to the right. Solving for y gives two branches, plus and minus three root x. The curve is a mirror image in the x axis. So the region inside the parabola up to a vertical line is twice the region under the upper branch. Symmetry halves the work.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: inside a parabola
slides.body_md: Find the area of the region bounded by $y^2 = 9x$ and the line $x = 4$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Upper branch $y = 3\sqrt{x}$; the line meets the parabola at $(4, \pm 6)$.

visual.alt: The parabola y squared equals 9 x opening to the right from the origin. The region inside it, up to the vertical line x equal to 4, is shaded; the line meets the parabola at (4, 6) and (4, minus 6).
visual.caption: The region is symmetric about the $x$-axis: twice the upper half.

slides.narration: Here the region is enclosed by the parabola y squared equals nine x and the vertical line x equals four. The upper branch is three root x. Double the integral from zero to four. The integral of root x is two thirds x to the power three halves, and four to the power three halves is eight. So the area is thirty two square units.

slides.heading: Horizontal strips: area beside the y-axis
slides.body_md: If the region lies between a curve and the **$y$-axis**, slice it horizontally. Write $x = g(y)$ and integrate with respect to $y$.

visual.alt: The right half of the parabola y equals x squared. The region between the curve and the y-axis, from the horizontal line y equal to 1 up to y equal to 4, is shaded; its corners on the curve are (1, 1) and (2, 4).
visual.caption: Horizontal strips of length $x = \sqrt{y}$ from $y = 1$ to $y = 4$.

slides.narration: Some regions sit beside the y axis, between two horizontal lines. Vertical strips would be awkward there, because they would not all reach the same curve. Use horizontal strips instead. Each has width d y and length x, so you write x in terms of y and integrate between the two y values.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: horizontal strips
slides.body_md: Find the area of the region in the first quadrant bounded by $y = x^2$, the $y$-axis and the lines $y = 1$ and $y = 4$.

visual.alt: The right half of the parabola y equals x squared. The region between the curve and the y-axis, from the horizontal line y equal to 1 up to y equal to 4, is shaded; its corners on the curve are (1, 1) and (2, 4).
visual.caption: Horizontal strips of length $x = \sqrt{y}$ from $y = 1$ to $y = 4$.

slides.narration: The region lies between the parabola and the y axis, from y equals one to y equals four. In the first quadrant, x equals root y. Integrate root y from one to four to get two thirds of eight minus one, which is fourteen over three square units. Notice that the limits are y values, read from the horizontal lines.

slides.heading: Quick check: negative integrals
slides.body_md: True or false? Think about the sign of each strip.

visual.alt: The downward parabola y equals minus x squared. The region between it and the x-axis, from x equal to 0 to x equal to 2, is shaded below the axis, ending at the point (2, minus 4).
visual.caption: $\displaystyle\int_0^2 (-x^2)\,dx = -\dfrac83$, but the shaded area is $\dfrac83$.

slides.narration: Decide whether the statement on the screen is true or false. Remember what happens to each strip when the curve is below the axis, and what an area must always be.

slides.heading: The recipe for every area question
slides.body_md: Follow the same steps every time; the sketch decides everything else.

nodes.label: Sketch the curve and the bounding lines; shade the region
Choose vertical strips ($dx$) or horizontal strips ($dy$)
Read the limits from the sketch
Use symmetry: one part times the number of equal parts
Integrate; split where the curve crosses the axis
Take absolute values and write sq units

visual.alt: Flow chart for any area question: sketch and shade the region, choose vertical or horizontal strips, read the limits, use symmetry, integrate while splitting at axis crossings, and finish with absolute values and square units.
visual.caption: The six-step recipe for every area question.

slides.narration: Here is a recipe that works for every question in this chapter. Sketch and shade the region. Choose vertical or horizontal strips. Read the limits from the sketch. Use symmetry if the region has equal parts. Integrate, splitting wherever the curve crosses the axis. Finally, give a positive answer in square units.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
slides.body_md: Areas under lines and parabolas.

visual.alt: Summary table: area under a non-negative curve is the integral; below the axis take the absolute value; when the curve crosses the axis at c add the absolute values of the two parts; beside the y-axis integrate x as a function of y; for a sideways parabola up to x equal to h double the upper-half integral.
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance.

slides.narration: To sum up. Area under a curve above the axis is the definite integral. Below the axis, take the absolute value. If the curve crosses the axis, split at the crossing point and add the absolute values. Beside the y axis, integrate x in terms of y. For a sideways parabola, double the upper half.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: Always draw a **sketch** and shade the region; it earns a mark
Find **where the curve crosses the axis** before integrating
Write the curve as $y = f(x)$ or $x = g(y)$ before integrating
End with a positive value and **sq units**
Area between two curves is **not** in the 2026–27 syllabus; every region here has one curve

visual.alt: Exam tips table: marks go for a correct sketch with the region shaded, the set-up of integrand and limits, the evaluation of the antiderivative, and a positive final answer with square units.
visual.caption: Where the marks are in an area question.

slides.narration: Final tips. A neat sketch with the region shaded usually carries a mark, so never skip it. Check for crossings before you integrate. Rewrite the curve in the form you need. Finish with a positive answer and the words square units. And remember that the area between two curves has been removed from this year's syllabus.

decks.title: Application of Integrals — Part 2: Areas of circles and ellipses
goals: Write the upper half of a circle or an ellipse as a function
Use the standard integral of the square root of a² − x²
Prove the areas πa² and πab by integration
Find areas of pieces cut off by lines parallel to an axis
Choose the slicing and symmetry factor for a region

slides.heading: Application of Integrals, Part 2
slides.body_md: Circles and ellipses: the area formulas you know, now proved.

visual.alt: The circle x squared plus y squared equals 16 centred at the origin, with the quarter in the first quadrant shaded, between (0, 4) on the y-axis and (4, 0) on the x-axis.
visual.caption: The shaded quarter has area $\displaystyle\int_0^4 \sqrt{16 - x^2}\,dx = 4\pi$.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. You have used pi r squared for years. Now you will prove it by integration, find the area of an ellipse, and then go further, finding the areas of pieces of circles and ellipses that no school formula covers. The shaded quarter on the screen is where every one of these calculations starts.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Write the **upper half** of a circle or ellipse as $y = \ldots$
Find **pieces** cut off by lines $x = h$

visual.alt: Table of the key standard integral: the integral of the square root of a squared minus x squared equals x over 2 times that root plus a squared over 2 times sine inverse of x over a, plus C. From 0 to a it equals pi a squared over 4.
visual.caption: The one integral this part needs.

slides.narration: Here are your goals for part two. You will turn a circle or an ellipse into a function, use one standard integral again and again, prove the two area formulas, and find areas of pieces cut off by vertical lines. Most five mark questions in this chapter come from this part.

slides.heading: A circle as two functions
slides.body_md: $x^2 + y^2 = a^2$ is not a function, but its **upper half** is: $y = \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$ for $-a \le x \le a$. The lower half is $y = -\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$.

visual.alt: The circle x squared plus y squared equals 36 drawn as two halves, the upper half y equals root of 36 minus x squared and the lower half its negative. It passes through (0, 6) and (0, minus 6).
visual.caption: Four equal quarters: area $= 4 \times 9\pi = 36\pi$.

slides.narration: A whole circle is not the graph of a function, because each x gives two y values. Split it. The upper half is y equals the square root of a squared minus x squared, and the lower half is the negative of that. The circle is symmetric about both axes, so its area is four times the area of the quarter in the first quadrant.

slides.heading: The standard integral
slides.body_md: This one antiderivative handles every circle and ellipse question.

visual.alt: Table of the key standard integral: the integral of the square root of a squared minus x squared equals x over 2 times that root plus a squared over 2 times sine inverse of x over a, plus C. From 0 to a it equals pi a squared over 4.
visual.caption: The one integral this part needs.

slides.narration: Here is the integral you need, from the chapter on integrals. The integral of root a squared minus x squared is x over two times the root, plus a squared over two times sine inverse of x over a. From zero to a, the first term vanishes at both ends, and sine inverse of one is pi over two. So a quarter circle has area pi a squared over four.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: area of a circle
slides.body_md: Using integration, find the area enclosed by the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 36$.
bullets: **Step 3 —** $= 4\left(0 + 18 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 36\pi$ sq units, which is $\pi r^2$ with $r = 6$.

visual.alt: The circle x squared plus y squared equals 36 drawn as two halves, the upper half y equals root of 36 minus x squared and the lower half its negative. It passes through (0, 6) and (0, minus 6).
visual.caption: Four equal quarters: area $= 4 \times 9\pi = 36\pi$.

slides.narration: For the circle with radius six, take four times the first quarter. Substitute six into the standard antiderivative. The root term is zero, and eighteen times sine inverse of one is eighteen times pi over two, which is nine pi. Four times nine pi is thirty six pi, exactly pi r squared. Integration agrees with the formula you already knew.

slides.heading: Quick check: a whole circle
slides.body_md: Use integration or the formula, but be sure it is the area.

visual.alt: The circle x squared plus y squared equals 16 centred at the origin, with the quarter in the first quadrant shaded, between (0, 4) on the y-axis and (4, 0) on the x-axis.
visual.caption: The shaded quarter has area $\displaystyle\int_0^4 \sqrt{16 - x^2}\,dx = 4\pi$.

slides.narration: Try this. One option is the circumference, not the area, and another squares the wrong number. Find the radius first.

slides.heading: An ellipse as two functions
slides.body_md: From $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$: $y = \pm\dfrac ba\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$. The upper half is the circle's upper half **squashed** by the factor $\dfrac ba$.

visual.alt: The ellipse x squared over 49 plus y squared over 16 equals 1, drawn as an upper and a lower half. It is 14 units wide and 8 units tall, passing through (0, 4) and (0, minus 4).
visual.caption: Semi-axes $a = 7$ and $b = 4$: area $\pi ab = 28\pi$.

slides.narration: Solve the ellipse equation for y. You get plus or minus b over a times root a squared minus x squared. So every height of the ellipse is the height of a circle of radius a, scaled by b over a. The area is scaled by the same factor. Pi a squared times b over a gives pi a b, the area of any ellipse.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: area of an ellipse
slides.body_md: Find the area enclosed by $\dfrac{x^2}{49} + \dfrac{y^2}{16} = 1$.

visual.alt: The ellipse x squared over 49 plus y squared over 16 equals 1, drawn as an upper and a lower half. It is 14 units wide and 8 units tall, passing through (0, 4) and (0, minus 4).
visual.caption: Semi-axes $a = 7$ and $b = 4$: area $\pi ab = 28\pi$.

slides.narration: Here a is seven and b is four. The upper half is four sevenths of root forty nine minus x squared. Four times the first quadrant integral gives sixteen sevenths times forty nine pi over four, which simplifies to twenty eight pi. That matches pi times seven times four. In an exam, show the integral even if you know the answer.

slides.heading: Quick check: a quarter circle
slides.body_md: How much of the circle is in one quadrant?

visual.alt: The circle x squared plus y squared equals 16 centred at the origin, with the quarter in the first quadrant shaded, between (0, 4) on the y-axis and (4, 0) on the x-axis.
visual.caption: The shaded quarter has area $\displaystyle\int_0^4 \sqrt{16 - x^2}\,dx = 4\pi$.

slides.narration: Here is a quick one. Find the area of the part of a circle that lies in the first quadrant. Think about what fraction of the whole circle that is.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a piece of a circle
slides.body_md: Find the area of the smaller region cut off from the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 16$ by the line $x = 2$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** The piece is right of $x = 2$, symmetric about the $x$-axis: $A = 2\displaystyle\int_2^4 \sqrt{16 - x^2}\,dx$.

visual.alt: The circle x squared plus y squared equals 16 with the dashed vertical line x equal to 2. The small piece of the circle to the right of the line is shaded; the line meets the circle at (2, 2 root 3) and (2, minus 2 root 3).
visual.caption: The smaller piece cut off by $x = 2$: twice the part above the axis.

slides.narration: Now something no school formula gives directly. The line x equals two cuts a small piece off the circle of radius four. It is symmetric about the x axis, so take twice the integral from two to four. At four the bracket is four pi. At two it is two root three plus four pi over three. Subtract and double: sixteen pi over three minus four root three.

slides.heading: Reading the limits from the figure
slides.body_md: The vertical line $x = 2$ meets the circle at $(2, \pm 2\sqrt{3})$; the piece runs from $x = 2$ to $x = 4$.

visual.alt: The circle x squared plus y squared equals 16 with the dashed vertical line x equal to 2. The small piece of the circle to the right of the line is shaded; the line meets the circle at (2, 2 root 3) and (2, minus 2 root 3).
visual.caption: The smaller piece cut off by $x = 2$: twice the part above the axis.

slides.narration: Look at the figure again. The dashed line x equals two meets the circle where y squared equals sixteen minus four, so y is plus or minus two root three. The shaded piece runs from x equals two to x equals four, which gives the limits. The sketch tells you both the limits and the symmetry factor.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a strip of an ellipse
slides.body_md: Find the area in the first quadrant under $\dfrac{x^2}{16} + \dfrac{y^2}{9} = 1$ between $x = 0$ and $x = 2$.

visual.alt: The first-quadrant quarter of the ellipse x squared over 16 plus y squared over 9 equals 1, from (0, 3) to (4, 0). The strip under it from x equal to 0 to x equal to 2 is shaded.
visual.caption: Area of the strip: $\dfrac34\displaystyle\int_0^2 \sqrt{16 - x^2}\,dx$.

slides.narration: This time take a strip of an ellipse. The upper half is three quarters of root sixteen minus x squared. Evaluate the standard antiderivative from zero to two: two root three plus four pi over three. Multiply by three quarters to get three root three over two plus pi, about five point seven four square units. No symmetry factor is needed, because only one quadrant is asked for.

slides.heading: Quick check: the upper half
slides.body_md: Which equation describes the top half of the circle?

visual.alt: The circle x squared plus y squared equals 36 drawn as two halves, the upper half y equals root of 36 minus x squared and the lower half its negative. It passes through (0, 6) and (0, minus 6).
visual.caption: Four equal quarters: area $= 4 \times 9\pi = 36\pi$.

slides.narration: Which function gives the upper half of the circle on the screen? Solve for y and choose the sign that keeps y positive.

slides.heading: Choosing the set-up
slides.body_md: Before integrating, decide the slicing, the limits and the symmetry factor.

visual.alt: Table of set-ups: a full circle or ellipse uses four times the first-quadrant integral; a piece cut off by the line x equals h uses twice the integral from h to a; a region beside the y-axis uses horizontal strips; a sideways parabola up to x equals h uses twice the upper-half integral.
visual.caption: Pick the slicing that gives one simple integral.

slides.narration: Here is how to set up the common regions. A full circle or ellipse is four times the first quadrant. A piece cut off by a vertical line is twice the integral from the line to the edge. A region beside the y axis uses horizontal strips. A sideways parabola is twice its upper half. Choose the set-up that leaves one simple integral.

slides.heading: Quick check: compare two areas
slides.body_md: True or false? Compare using the formulas.

visual.alt: The ellipse x squared over 49 plus y squared over 16 equals 1, drawn as an upper and a lower half. It is 14 units wide and 8 units tall, passing through (0, 4) and (0, minus 4).
visual.caption: Semi-axes $a = 7$ and $b = 4$: area $\pi ab = 28\pi$.

slides.narration: Is the statement true or false? Work out both areas, the ellipse with pi a b and the circle with pi r squared, and compare them carefully. A wider shape is not always the larger one.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2
slides.body_md: Circles and ellipses.

visual.alt: Summary table: for the circle x squared plus y squared equals a squared, the upper half is root of a squared minus x squared and the area is pi a squared; for the ellipse the upper half is b over a times that root and the area is pi a b.
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance.

slides.narration: To sum up. Write the upper half of a circle or ellipse as a function of x. Use the standard integral of root a squared minus x squared. A circle encloses pi a squared and an ellipse pi a b. For a piece cut off by a vertical line, integrate from the line to the edge, and multiply by two for the half below the axis.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 2
bullets: Draw the curve and the cutting line; mark where they meet
Write the **symmetry factor** before the integral
Leave answers exact, such as $\dfrac{16\pi}{3} - 4\sqrt{3}$, unless a decimal is asked for
Convert equations such as $9x^2 + 25y^2 = 225$ to standard form first

rows: areas are positive; write sq units

visual.alt: Exam tips table of common slips: counting only the upper half, so multiply by 2 or 4; writing a over b instead of b over a, so solve for y carefully; using degrees for sine inverse, so use radians; and leaving a negative answer, so remember areas are positive with square units.
visual.caption: Four slips that cost marks.

slides.narration: Final tips for part two. Sketch the curve and the cutting line and mark where they meet. Write the symmetry factor before the integral sign. Use radians for sine inverse. Leave exact answers unless a decimal is asked for. And always divide to reach standard form before reading off a and b.

notes.title: Application of Integrals — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Area under a curve
sections.body_md:
If $f$ is continuous and $f(x) \ge 0$ on $[a, b]$, the area of the region bounded by $y = f(x)$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x = a$, $x = b$ is

$$A = \int_a^b y\,dx = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

Think of the region as many thin vertical strips of height $y$ and width $dx$. Example: under $y = 2x + 1$ from $x = 1$ to $x = 3$ the area is $\left[x^2 + x\right]_1^3 = 10$ sq units, which is also the area of the trapezium with parallel sides $3$ and $7$ and width $2$.

key_terms.definition_md: A thin vertical strip of height $y$ and width $dx$ (area $y\,dx$), or a horizontal strip of length $x$ and width $dy$.
The vertical lines $x = a$ and $x = b$ that bound the region.

sections.heading: 2. Curves below the axis and curves that cross it
sections.body_md:
If $f(x) \le 0$ on $[a, b]$, the integral is negative and the area is $\left|\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\right|$.

If the curve crosses the axis at $x = c$ inside $[a, b]$, **split** there and add absolute values:

$$A = \left|\int_a^c f(x)\,dx\right| + \left|\int_c^b f(x)\,dx\right|.$$

Example: $y = 2x - 4$ on $[0, 4]$ crosses at $x = 2$; the parts are $4$ and $4$, so the area is $8$, although $\displaystyle\int_0^4 (2x - 4)\,dx = 0$.

key_terms.definition_md: The value of the definite integral: parts below the axis count as negative.

formulas.label: Curve crossing the axis at c

visual.alt: Two shaded triangles between the line y equals 2 x minus 4 and the x-axis: one below the axis from x equal to 0 to 2, one above the axis from 2 to 4. Each has area 4.

sections.heading: 3. Horizontal strips: area beside the y-axis
sections.body_md:
For the region between a curve $x = g(y) \ge 0$, the $y$-axis and the lines $y = c$, $y = d$:

$$A = \int_c^d x\,dy = \int_c^d g(y)\,dy.$$

Example: the region in the first quadrant beside $y = x^2$ from $y = 1$ to $y = 4$ has $x = \sqrt{y}$ and area $\dfrac23(8 - 1) = \dfrac{14}{3}$ sq units. The limits are $y$-values.

key_terms.definition_md: A strip of length $x = g(y)$ and width $dy$.

sections.heading: 4. Parabolas in standard form
sections.body_md:
- $x^2 = ky$ ($k > 0$): $y = \dfrac{x^2}{k}$, a U symmetric about the $y$-axis. Area under it from $0$ to $h$: $\dfrac{h^3}{3k}$.
- $y^2 = kx$ ($k > 0$): branches $y = \pm\sqrt{kx}$, symmetric about the $x$-axis. The region cut off by $x = h$ has area $2\displaystyle\int_0^h \sqrt{kx}\,dx = \dfrac43\sqrt{k}\,h^{3/2}$.

Example: $y^2 = 9x$ and $x = 4$: $2\displaystyle\int_0^4 3\sqrt{x}\,dx = 32$ sq units. This equals two-thirds of the enclosing rectangle ($4 \times 12$), a useful check.

key_terms.definition_md: A line about which the region is a mirror image; it lets you integrate one part and multiply.

sections.heading: 5. Circles
sections.body_md:
Upper half of $x^2 + y^2 = a^2$: $y = \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$. The key integral is

$$\int \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\,dx = \frac x2\sqrt{a^2 - x^2} + \frac{a^2}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac xa + C.$$

Quarter circle: $\displaystyle\int_0^a \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\,dx = \dfrac{\pi a^2}{4}$, so the circle encloses $\pi a^2$. A piece cut off by $x = h$ ($0 < h < a$) has area $2\displaystyle\int_h^a \sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\,dx$; for $a = 4$, $h = 2$ this is $\dfrac{16\pi}{3} - 4\sqrt{3}$.

key_terms.definition_md: The part of the curve with $y \ge 0$, written as a function of $x$.

visuals.caption: The smaller piece cut off by $x = 2$: twice the part above the axis.

sections.heading: 6. Ellipses
sections.body_md:
From $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$: upper half $y = \dfrac ba\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$. By symmetry,

$$A = 4\int_0^a \frac ba\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\,dx = \pi ab.$$

Convert to standard form first: $9x^2 + 25y^2 = 225$ becomes $\dfrac{x^2}{25} + \dfrac{y^2}{9} = 1$, so the area is $15\pi$. A strip of an ellipse uses the same standard integral, e.g. $\dfrac34\displaystyle\int_0^2 \sqrt{16 - x^2}\,dx = \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} + \pi$.

key_terms.definition_md: $a$ and $b$ in $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$: half the width and half the height.

visual.alt: The ellipse x squared over 49 plus y squared over 16 equals 1, drawn as an upper and a lower half. It is 14 units wide and 8 units tall, passing through (0, 4) and (0, minus 4).
visual.caption: Semi-axes $a = 7$ and $b = 4$: area $\pi ab = 28\pi$.

visuals.alt: The first-quadrant quarter of the ellipse x squared over 16 plus y squared over 9 equals 1, from (0, 3) to (4, 0). The strip under it from x equal to 0 to x equal to 2 is shaded.
visuals.caption: Area of the strip: $\dfrac34\displaystyle\int_0^2 \sqrt{16 - x^2}\,dx$.

sections.heading: 7. Choosing the method; what is not in the syllabus
sections.body_md:
1. Sketch and shade the region; mark where the curve meets the bounding lines.
2. Choose vertical strips ($dx$) or horizontal strips ($dy$).
3. Read the limits; note any axis crossing.
4. Use symmetry (factor $2$ or $4$).
5. Integrate, take absolute values, write sq units.

*Not in the 2026–27 syllabus:* the area **between two curves** (for example between a parabola and a slanting line, or between two circles). Every region in this chapter is bounded by one curve together with the axes or lines parallel to them.

key_terms.definition_md: The number of equal parts of the region: integrate one and multiply.

visual.alt: Table of set-ups: a full circle or ellipse uses four times the first-quadrant integral; a piece cut off by the line x equals h uses twice the integral from h to a; a region beside the y-axis uses horizontal strips; a sideways parabola up to x equals h uses twice the upper-half integral.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Area question (3–5 marks):* sketch with the region shaded (1), correct integrand and limits (1–2), antiderivative and substitution (1–2), final positive answer with sq units (1).
- *Objective (1 mark):* recognising the formula $\pi ab$, the symmetry factor or the effect of a crossing.
- *Case-based (4 marks):* read the curve from the context, set up one integral, interpret the answer (cost, equal division).

**Common mistakes**
1. Integrating straight across a point where the curve crosses the axis, so the parts cancel.
2. Leaving a negative answer for a region below the axis.
3. Wrong limits: using $y$-values with $dx$ or $x$-values with $dy$.
4. Forgetting the symmetry factor $2$ or $4$ (counting only the upper half).
5. Writing $\dfrac ab$ instead of $\dfrac ba$ for the ellipse's upper half.
6. Using degrees in $\sin^{-1}$: $\sin^{-1} 1 = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$, not $90$.
7. Not converting $9x^2 + 25y^2 = 225$ to standard form before reading $a$ and $b$.
8. Missing "sq units" in the final line.

questions.stem_md: Let $f$ be continuous and $f(x) \ge 0$ on $[a, b]$. The area of the region bounded by $y = f(x)$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x = a$ and $x = b$ is
questions.solution_md: Add up thin vertical strips of height $f(x)$ and width $dx$. Option (c) equals option (b), the change in $f$, not an area.

questions.stem_md: The area of the region bounded by the line $y = 4x$, the $x$-axis and the ordinate $x = 3$ is
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^3 4x\,dx = \left[2x^2\right]_0^3 = 18$. It is also a triangle with base $3$ and height $12$: $\tfrac12 \times 3 \times 12 = 18$. Option (c) forgets the half.

questions.stem_md: What is the area under the parabola $y = 3x^2$ from $x = 1$ to $x = 2$, above the $x$-axis?
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_1^2 3x^2\,dx = \left[x^3\right]_1^2 = 8 - 1 = 7$. Option (b) forgets the lower limit.

questions.stem_md: The region bounded by the curve $y = \sqrt{x}$, the $x$-axis and the line $x = 9$ has area
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^9 x^{1/2}\,dx = \tfrac23\left[x^{3/2}\right]_0^9 = \tfrac23 \times 27 = 18$. Option (a) forgets the factor $\tfrac23$.

questions.stem_md: The line $y = x - 3$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x = 3$. The area enclosed by this line, the $x$-axis and the lines $x = 0$ and $x = 6$ is
questions.solution_md: The line is below the axis on $(0, 3)$ and above it on $(3, 6)$. Area $= \left|\displaystyle\int_0^3 (x - 3)\,dx\right| + \displaystyle\int_3^6 (x - 3)\,dx = 4.5 + 4.5 = 9$. Option (b) is the signed integral, in which the two parts cancel.

questions.stem_md: Using integration, the area enclosed by the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 25$ is
questions.solution_md: Area $= 4\displaystyle\int_0^5 \sqrt{25 - x^2}\,dx = 4 \times \dfrac{25\pi}{4} = 25\pi$, which agrees with $\pi r^2$ for $r = 5$. Option (d) is the circumference.

questions.stem_md: The ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{36} + \dfrac{y^2}{25} = 1$ encloses a region of area
questions.solution_md: Here $a = 6$ and $b = 5$, so the area is $\pi ab = 30\pi$. Options (d) and (a) add the semi-axes or the squares instead of multiplying.

questions.stem_md: The part of the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 64$ that lies in the first quadrant has area
questions.solution_md: $\displaystyle\int_0^8 \sqrt{64 - x^2}\,dx = \dfrac{\pi \cdot 64}{4} = 16\pi$, one quarter of the full circle $64\pi$.

questions.stem_md: Using horizontal strips, find the area of the region bounded by the parabola $x = y^2$, the $y$-axis and the lines $y = 0$ and $y = 3$.
questions.solution_md: Each horizontal strip has length $x = y^2$ and width $dy$: area $= \displaystyle\int_0^3 y^2\,dy = \left[\dfrac{y^3}{3}\right]_0^3 = 9$.

questions.stem_md: The region enclosed between the parabola $y^2 = 16x$ and the vertical line $x = 1$ (both above and below the $x$-axis) has area
questions.solution_md: The upper half is $y = 4\sqrt{x}$. By symmetry, area $= 2\displaystyle\int_0^1 4\sqrt{x}\,dx = 8 \times \dfrac23 = \dfrac{16}{3}$. Option (c) is only the upper half.

questions.stem_md: Which integral gives the area enclosed by the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{16} + \dfrac{y^2}{4} = 1$?
questions.solution_md: Upper half: $y = \tfrac24\sqrt{16 - x^2} = \tfrac12\sqrt{16 - x^2}$, for $0 \le x \le 4$ in the first quadrant. questions.stem_md: $\displaystyle\int_{-3}^{3} x\,dx$ equals the area bounded by $y = x$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x = -3$ and $x = 3$.

questions.stem_md: The area of the rectangle-shaped region bounded by $y = 5$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x = 1$, $x = 4$ is ____ square units.

questions.stem_md: Under the curve $y = x^2$, between $x = 0$ and $x = 3$ and above the $x$-axis, the area is ____ square units.
questions.solution_md: $\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^3 = 9$.

questions.stem_md: The ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1$ encloses $k\pi$ square units, where $k =$ ____.
questions.solution_md: $a = 2$, $b = 1$: area $\pi ab = 2\pi$.

questions.stem_md: The region enclosed by the parabola $y^2 = x$ and the line $x = 4$ has area ____ square units.
questions.solution_md: $2\displaystyle\int_0^4 \sqrt{x}\,dx = 2 \cdot \dfrac23 \cdot 8 = \dfrac{32}{3}$, i.e. 32/3.

questions.stem_md: Prove, by integration, that the region enclosed by $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ ($a, b > 0$) has area $\pi ab$.

answer.model_answer_md:

$= \dfrac{4b}{a} \cdot \dfrac{a^2}{2} \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2} = \pi ab$.

questions.stem_md: Using integration, find the area of the smaller region cut off from the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 36$ by the line $x = 3$.

answer.model_answer_md:
The smaller region lies to the right of $x = 3$ and is symmetric about the $x$-axis. Upper boundary: $y = \sqrt{36 - x^2}$.

Area $= 2\displaystyle\int_3^6 \sqrt{36 - x^2}\,dx = 2\left[\dfrac x2\sqrt{36 - x^2} + 18\sin^{-1}\dfrac x6\right]_3^6$

At $x = 6$: $0 + 18 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2} = 9\pi$. At $x = 3$: $\dfrac32\sqrt{27} + 18 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{2} + 3\pi$.

Area $= 2\left(6\pi - \dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 12\pi - 9\sqrt{3} \approx 22.11$ sq units.

questions.stem_md: Find the area of the region in the first quadrant bounded by the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{36} + \dfrac{y^2}{16} = 1$, the coordinate axes and the line $x = 3$. Also find what fraction of the ellipse's first-quadrant area this is, to two decimal places.

answer.model_answer_md:
Upper half: $y = \dfrac23\sqrt{36 - x^2}$.

Area $= \dfrac23\displaystyle\int_0^3 \sqrt{36 - x^2}\,dx = \dfrac23\left[\dfrac x2\sqrt{36 - x^2} + 18\sin^{-1}\dfrac x6\right]_0^3 = \dfrac23\left(\dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{2} + 3\pi\right) = 3\sqrt{3} + 2\pi \approx 11.48$ sq units.

First-quadrant area of the ellipse $= \dfrac{\pi \times 6 \times 4}{4} = 6\pi \approx 18.85$. Fraction $\approx \dfrac{11.48}{18.85} \approx 0.61$.

questions.stem_md:
Find the area of the region in the first quadrant bounded by the parabola $x^2 = 2y$, the $y$-axis and the line $y = 8$

(a) using horizontal strips, and

(b) using vertical strips, as a rectangle minus the area under the curve. Show that the answers agree.

answer.model_answer_md:
The parabola meets $y = 8$ where $x^2 = 16$, i.e. at $(4, 8)$.

(a) $x = \sqrt{2y}$: area $= \displaystyle\int_0^8 \sqrt{2}\,y^{1/2}\,dy = \sqrt{2} \cdot \dfrac23 \cdot 8^{3/2} = \sqrt{2} \cdot \dfrac23 \cdot 16\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{64}{3}$ sq units.

(b) Rectangle $0 \le x \le 4$, $0 \le y \le 8$ has area $32$. Area under the curve: $\displaystyle\int_0^4 \dfrac{x^2}{2}\,dx = \dfrac{64}{6} = \dfrac{32}{3}$. Required area $= 32 - \dfrac{32}{3} = \dfrac{64}{3}$ sq units. The two methods agree.

$= \dfrac{12}{5} \cdot \dfrac{25}{2} \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2} = 15\pi$ sq units.

By symmetry, the second-quadrant part is $\dfrac{15\pi}{4}$ sq units.
